title: Enough
hook: contentment is the greatest wealth (Dhammapada 204); greed makes any amount too little

segments.voice: Yesterday: Baizhang, still working the fields in old age. Work is practice, done with your whole attention.

There was once a king, the old stories say, who could make it rain money. He'd clap his hands, and gold coins would fall from the sky until they were knee-deep. He ruled the whole earth. Then he wanted heaven, and got it: first the heaven of the four great kings, then the higher heaven where Sakka, king of the gods, gave him half his throne. And sitting on half a throne in paradise, King Mandhatu had one small thought: why only half?
screen: `A KING WHO MAKES IT RAIN GOLD.` → `HALF A THRONE IN HEAVEN.` → `WHY ONLY HALF?`

segments.voice: The moment he thought it, the story says, his power drained away. He fell back to earth, into his own garden, an old man, and died there. The tradition tells this story alongside a short verse of the Dhammapada. In Max Müller's translation: "There is no satisfying lusts, even by a shower of gold pieces." That's Mandhatu's rain. He didn't want something wicked. Wanting simply has no built-in stopping point: whatever you have, greed can make it feel too little. A raise feels like enough for a while, then the new number becomes the floor. Another verse, which you may remember from the first year, gives the alternative in four words. Müller has it: "contentedness the best riches." The Pali is santuṭṭhi: contentment, being satisfied with what's here. It's called riches, not poverty. Contentment isn't settling for less, and it isn't a ban on ever wanting anything. In this tradition it's a wealth you can actually keep, because it doesn't depend on the number. That closes six days on livelihood. Earn clean. Watch what your money does. Count blamelessness above it all. Divide it wisely. Work with your whole attention. And at some point, say the one word greed can't say: enough.
screen: `HE FALLS BACK TO EARTH.` · `NO SATISFYING IT, EVEN WITH GOLD.` · `THE NEW NUMBER BECOMES THE FLOOR.` · `CONTENTMENT IS RICHES.` · then, large: `ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Picture your home and pick one thing, a coat, your bed, the food in your kitchen, and say quietly: this is enough. If something inside argues, let it talk and stay with the thing anyway, then try the breath itself: this breath is enough.
Enough. Santuṭṭhi, contentment: the Dhammapada calls it the best riches, because greed can make any amount feel too little.
Your line: contentment is the best riches. It's a wealth that doesn't depend on the number. Till tomorrow.

howItsDone: Buddhist texts praise contentment often; monastics practice it by living with a few requisites, and lay Buddhists often reflect on it when they recite or study the Dhammapada and the Mangala Sutta, which lists contentment among the highest blessings.
